blocks.content: Once you know what to build, the next question is the most important one in the whole design: what are the main things in this system? Those things become your classes, and finding them well is the foundation everything else rests on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974114534-771560469.png

An entity is a core concept in the problem that has its own identity and its own data. In a parking lot, a Vehicle is an entity, a Ticket is an entity, a Spot is an entity. Each one is a noun you can point at.
Get the entities right and the design almost writes itself. Get them wrong, either too many or too few, and you will fight your own structure for the rest of the interview.

blocks.title: The goal of this step
blocks.content: Turn the requirements into a clean list of the classes your system needs, each one focused and clearly named.
1. What Counts as an Entity
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972210078-768444585.png
blocks.alt: A concept with data and identity is an entity, else a value

blocks.content: An entity is usually something you can describe with data, and often with behaviour. It is a real concept in the problem, not a vague idea.

["It has its own identity, like a specific ticket or a specific user.","It holds data, such as a number plate or a slot number.","It often has behaviour, like a ticket working out its own duration.","It maps to a noun you would use when explaining the system out loud."]
items: It has its own identity, like a specific ticket or a specific user.
It holds data, such as a number plate or a slot number.
It often has behaviour, like a ticket working out its own duration.
It maps to a noun you would use when explaining the system out loud.

blocks.content: If you can say "the system has many of these, each with its own details", you are almost certainly looking at an entity.
The Noun Technique
The simplest and most reliable trick in all of LLD: read the requirements and underline the nouns. Nouns are candidate entities, and verbs are candidate methods.
This works because a system is mostly made of things (nouns) that do actions (verbs). The things become classes, the actions become the methods on them.

blocks.title: Nouns in a parking lot prompt
blocks.text: A vehicle enters the parking lot through a gate, takes a ticket, parks in a slot on a level, and pays a fee on exit. Nouns: vehicle, parking lot, gate, ticket, slot, level, fee.

blocks.content: In one reading you already have a strong first draft of entities. You then trim, group, and refine that list.
2. A Worked Pass Over the Nouns
blocks.text: 2. A Worked Pass Over the Nouns

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972212351-715714776.png
blocks.alt: Turning the nouns into entities, Fee is only a value

blocks.content: Let us take those parking lot nouns and decide what each becomes.

{"headers":["Noun","Becomes","Why"],"rows":[["Vehicle","Entity","Has a plate and a type, many exist"],["Ticket","Entity","Has identity and an entry time"],["Slot","Entity","Has a number and a free or busy state"],["Level","Entity","Groups many slots"],["Fee","Value","Just an amount, no identity of its own"],["Gate","Entity","Has behaviour, issues and scans tickets"]]}
Notice that not every noun becomes a full entity. Fee is just a number, so it is a value, not a class with identity. This judgement is exactly what the interviewer wants to see.
Core vs Supporting Entities
Not all entities are equally important. Separate the few central ones from the many small helpers, and design the core first.

{"headers":["Kind","Role","Example in a parking lot"],"rows":[["Core","The heart of the system","ParkingLot, Slot, Ticket, Vehicle"],["Supporting","Helpers around the core","Gate, Payment, PricingRule"]]}

blocks.title: Design order
blocks.content: Get the core entities solid first. Supporting entities can be added once the backbone is clear, and it keeps you from drowning in detail early.
3. Entity vs Value Object
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972213990-493468053.png
blocks.alt: Identity important means entity, otherwise value object

blocks.content: This distinction quietly separates strong candidates from the rest. Some concepts have identity, others are just values.
An entity has identity
A User is an entity. Two users with the same name are still different people. Identity means it matters which specific one you are talking about.
A value object is defined by its value
blocks.text: A value object is defined by its value

blocks.content: A Money amount of one hundred rupees is a value. One hundred rupees is one hundred rupees, it does not matter which one. Colours, dates, and coordinates are usually values.

codes.python:
class User:   # entity: identity matters
    def __init__(self, user_id, name):
        self.id = user_id
        self.name = name


class Money:   # value object: defined by its amount
    def __init__(self, amount, currency):
        self.amount = amount
        self.currency = currency

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.amount == other.amount and self.currency == other.currency


if __name__ == "__main__":
    alice = User("U-1", "Alice")
    bob = User("U-2", "Alice")   # same name, different identity

    price1 = Money(10000, "INR")
    price2 = Money(10000, "INR")   # same value, considered equal

    print(f"Alice id: {alice.id}, Bob id: {bob.id} (different identities, same name)")
    print(f"price1 equals price2 by value: {price1 == price2}")

blocks.content: Ask: if two of these have the same data, are they the same thing? If yes, it is a value. If no, it is an entity with identity.
Giving Entities Attributes
Once you have an entity, ask what data it holds. These become its fields. Keep them focused on what the entity truly owns.
Notice each entity holds only its own data. The Slot does not know about payments, and the Vehicle does not know about gates. That separation is the whole goal.
4. Giving Entities Behaviour
Entities are not just bags of data. They often own the behaviour that acts on their own data. This keeps logic close to where it belongs.

blocks.title: A useful rule
blocks.content: If a method mostly uses one entity data, it usually belongs on that entity. A ticket knowing its own duration is more natural than a service reaching into the ticket to compute it.
5. Enums for Fixed Sets
When an attribute can only be one of a small fixed set of values, an enum is cleaner than loose text. It prevents typos and makes the options explicit.
Enums are a small touch that make a design feel professional, and they stop bugs where someone passes "car" one place and "Car" another.
6. Do Not Over Model
A common beginner mistake is inventing too many entities, creating a class for every tiny concept. This clutters the design and wastes precious time.
If a concept has no data and no behaviour of its own, it probably does not need to be a class yet.
Start with the entities you clearly need for the agreed scope. You can always introduce more when a real need appears during the design.
7. Do Not Under Model Either
The opposite mistake is just as harmful: missing an entity and cramming its data into another class. This creates a bloated class doing several jobs.

blocks.title: A missed entity
blocks.text: If you store pricing rules as loose fields inside ParkingLot, that class now handles parking and pricing. Pulling pricing out into its own PricingRule entity keeps both clean.

blocks.content: When one class starts collecting unrelated fields, that is a sign a hidden entity is waiting to be pulled out.
8. Naming Entities Well
An entity name should be a clear, singular noun that anyone on the team would understand. Good names make the whole design readable.

["Use singular nouns: Ticket, not Tickets.","Be specific: ParkingSlot beats a vague Item.","Match the language of the domain, the words the users actually use.","Avoid technical noise like Manager or Data unless it truly means that."]
items: Use singular nouns: Ticket, not Tickets.
Be specific: ParkingSlot beats a vague Item.
Match the language of the domain, the words the users actually use.
Avoid technical noise like Manager or Data unless it truly means that.

blocks.content: 9. A Second Example: A Library System
blocks.text: 9. A Second Example: A Library System

blocks.content: To prove the technique is universal, apply it to a different prompt: design a library.

blocks.title: Library nouns
blocks.text: A member borrows a book copy from the library, and a librarian records the loan with a due date. Nouns: Member, Book, BookCopy, Library, Librarian, Loan.

blocks.content: Notice a subtle but important entity: Book versus BookCopy. A Book is the title, while a BookCopy is one physical copy on the shelf. Spotting that difference is exactly the skill this step builds.
10. From Entities to Classes
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974127355-295654410.png
blocks.alt: Library entities as a class diagram

blocks.content: Once your entity list is solid, turning it into class skeletons is quick. Each entity becomes a class with its fields and a few methods.

codes.python:
import time


class Book:
    def __init__(self, isbn, title):
        self.isbn = isbn
        self.title = title


class BookCopy:
    def __init__(self, copy_id, book):
        self.copy_id = copy_id
        self.book = book
        self.available = True


class Member:
    def __init__(self, member_id, name):
        self.id = member_id
        self.name = name
        self.loans = []


class Loan:
    def __init__(self, copy, member, due_date):
        self.copy = copy
        self.member = member
        self.due_date = due_date


if __name__ == "__main__":
    book = Book("978-0132350884", "Clean Code")
    copy = BookCopy("C-1", book)
    member = Member("M-1", "Priya")

    copy.available = False
    due_date = time.time() + 14 * 24 * 60 * 60
    loan = Loan(copy, member, due_date)
    member.loans.append(loan)

    print(f"{member.name} borrowed \"{loan.copy.book.title}\" (copy {loan.copy.copy_id})")
    print(f"Copy available: {copy.available}")
    print(f"{member.name} has {len(member.loans)} active loan(s)")

blocks.content: With clear entities, the classes fall out naturally, and you are ready to connect them in the relationships step.
11. Attributes vs Behaviour
For each entity, decide what it knows (its data) and what it does (its behaviour). Data becomes fields, behaviour becomes methods, and keeping them on the right entity is what makes a design clean.

blocks.title: Ticket, split correctly
blocks.text: Knows: entry time, the vehicle, the slot. Does: work out its own duration. It does not know about pricing rules, because those change for different reasons.

blocks.content: When behaviour naturally acts on one entity data, put it on that entity. This keeps logic close to the data it uses and avoids anaemic classes that are just bags of fields.
12. Turning Verbs Into Methods
If nouns give you entities, verbs give you methods. Read the requirements again and underline the actions.

// "a vehicle parks", "a ticket is issued", "a fee is calculated"
// park(vehicle), issueTicket(vehicle), calculateFee(ticket)
blocks.code:
// "a vehicle parks", "a ticket is issued", "a fee is calculated"
// park(vehicle), issueTicket(vehicle), calculateFee(ticket)

codes.java:
// "a vehicle parks", "a ticket is issued", "a fee is calculated"
// park(vehicle), issueTicket(vehicle), calculateFee(ticket)
codes.python:
// "a vehicle parks", "a ticket is issued", "a fee is calculated"
// park(vehicle), issueTicket(vehicle), calculateFee(ticket)
codes.cpp:
// "a vehicle parks", "a ticket is issued", "a fee is calculated"
// park(vehicle), issueTicket(vehicle), calculateFee(ticket)

blocks.content: Each verb becomes a method on whichever entity or service owns that action. This pairing of nouns to classes and verbs to methods is the quiet engine of object oriented design.
13. A Third Example: Food Delivery
One more pass, on a food delivery app, to make the technique automatic.

blocks.title: Food delivery nouns
blocks.text: A customer places an order containing items from a restaurant, and a delivery agent delivers it. Entities: Customer, Order, OrderItem, Restaurant, MenuItem, DeliveryAgent.

blocks.content: Notice Order versus OrderItem, and MenuItem versus OrderItem. Spotting that a menu item and an ordered item are different concepts is exactly the modelling skill interviewers reward.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Underline the nouns first","Focus on core entities early","Give each entity only its own data","Use enums for fixed value sets","Tell entities apart from values"],"cons":["Inventing a class for everything","Cramming unrelated data into one entity","Modelling features out of scope","Loose text where an enum fits","Ignoring identity versus plain values"]}
15. Common Questions
How do I know if something should be a class? - Ask whether it has its own data or behaviour. If yes, it is likely a class. If it is just a label, it may be an enum or a simple value.

What is the difference between an entity and a value object? - An entity has identity and can change over time, like a User. A value object is defined only by its values, like a Money amount, and needs no identity.
How many entities should a design have? - Only as many as the scope needs. A tidy small design beats a sprawling one. Start with the core and extend later.
What if I miss an entity? - You will notice when one class starts holding unrelated data or doing several jobs. That is your cue to pull a hidden entity out.
16. Key Takeaways

["Entities are the core things in the system, and they become your classes.","Find them by underlining the nouns in the requirements.","Separate core entities from supporting ones, and design the core first.","Tell entities with identity apart from plain value objects.","Give each entity only its own data and behaviour.","Do not over model with too many classes, or under model by cramming."]
items: Entities are the core things in the system, and they become your classes.
Find them by underlining the nouns in the requirements.
Separate core entities from supporting ones, and design the core first.
Tell entities with identity apart from plain value objects.
Give each entity only its own data and behaviour.
Do not over model with too many classes, or under model by cramming.

blocks.content: With your entities identified, you have the building blocks. The next step is to connect them, working out how these classes relate to one another.
